case_facts_html:
X Ltd. purchased 3,000 shares of Amazing Ltd. in December 2023 @ ₹100 each and paid brokerage @ 1%. In May 2024, Amazing Ltd. issued bonus shares at one for every three shares held by shareholders.

X Ltd. sold 1000 shares in September 2024 at ₹110 each. After issue of bonus, shares were quoted at ₹95. In December 2024, the shares were quoted at ₹70.
question_html: What would be the carrying cost of investments in Amazing Ltd. after sale of shares as per AS 13:
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹2,27,250 — original cost = 3,000 shares × ₹100 + 1% brokerage = ₹3,03,000. The May 2024 bonus issue (1 for 3) adds 1,000 shares at nil cost, so the weighted-average cost across the enlarged 4,000-share holding remains ₹3,03,000, i.e. ₹75.75/share. On sale of 1,000 shares in September 2024, the cost removed = 1,000 × ₹75.75 = ₹75,750, leaving the carrying cost of the remaining 3,000 shares at ₹3,03,000 − ₹75,750 = ₹2,27,250.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.5): Weighted-average cost per share after a bonus issue, applied to shares sold

case_facts_html:
X Ltd. purchased 3,000 shares of Amazing Ltd. in December 2023 @ ₹100 each and paid brokerage @ 1%. In May 2024, Amazing Ltd. issued bonus shares at one for every three shares held by shareholders.

X Ltd. sold 1000 shares in September 2024 at ₹110 each. After issue of bonus, shares were quoted at ₹95. In December 2024, the shares were quoted at ₹70.
question_html: What is the cost of bonus shares:
answer_html: Answer: (C) Nil — bonus shares are not separately costed; the existing cost of the original holding (₹3,03,000) is simply spread over the enlarged number of shares (original 3,000 plus 1,000 bonus = 4,000), so the bonus shares themselves carry no incremental cost.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.5): Cost of bonus shares is nil, by analogy to AS 13's rights-share cost-spreading principle

case_facts_html:
X Ltd. purchased 3,000 shares of Amazing Ltd. in December 2023 @ ₹100 each and paid brokerage @ 1%. In May 2024, Amazing Ltd. issued bonus shares at one for every three shares held by shareholders.

X Ltd. sold 1000 shares in September 2024 at ₹110 each. After issue of bonus, shares were quoted at ₹95. In December 2024, the shares were quoted at ₹70.
question_html: What is the profit on sale of Bonus Shares:
answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹34,250 — using the weighted-average cost of ₹75.75/share (see Q2(a)), the cost of the 1,000 shares sold = ₹75,750; sale proceeds = 1,000 × ₹110 = ₹1,10,000; profit = ₹1,10,000 − ₹75,750 = ₹34,250.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.5): Profit on sale computed using the weighted-average cost basis across original and bonus shares

case_facts_html:
X Ltd. purchased 3,000 shares of Amazing Ltd. in December 2023 @ ₹100 each and paid brokerage @ 1%. In May 2024, Amazing Ltd. issued bonus shares at one for every three shares held by shareholders.

X Ltd. sold 1000 shares in September 2024 at ₹110 each. After issue of bonus, shares were quoted at ₹95. In December 2024, the shares were quoted at ₹70.
question_html: What would be the carrying cost of investments in Amazing Ltd. in quarter ending in December 2024 as per AS 13:
answer_html: Answer: (A) ₹2,10,000 — the remaining 3,000 shares carry a weighted-average cost of ₹2,27,250 (see Q2(a)); at the December 2024 market price of ₹70/share, their fair value = 3,000 × ₹70 = ₹2,10,000. As per AS 13, a current investment is carried at the lower of cost and fair value, so the carrying amount is written down to ₹2,10,000.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.6): Current investment carried at the lower of (weighted-average) cost and fair value

case_facts_html: Sun Limited has acquired 40% share in Moon Ltd. for ₹500,000 on 01.07.2023. Moon Ltd. is holding 40% stake in Star Limited. Now, sun limited can exercise significant influence on Moon Limited. Moon limited declared dividend of ₹80,000 for the Financial Year 2022-23 on 15.09.2023. For the year 2023-24, Moon Ltd. earned profit of ₹4,00,000 and declared dividend for ₹90,000 on 15.09.2024.
question_html: What will be the carrying amount of investment in Separate Financial Statements of Sun Limited as on 31.03.2024?
answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹4,68,000 — in Sun's separate financial statements, the investment is carried at cost. The dividend of ₹80,000 declared on 15.09.2023 relates to Moon's FY2022-23 profits, a pre-acquisition period (Sun acquired its stake on 01.07.2023); Sun's 40% share of this pre-acquisition dividend (₹32,000) is treated as a recovery of the cost of investment, not as income, reducing the carrying cost to ₹5,00,000 − ₹32,000 = ₹4,68,000.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.5): Separate financial statements: a pre-acquisition dividend received is deducted from the cost of investment

question_html: Cost of current investment acquired was ₹1000 but the fair value was ₹800. The Investment was recorded at ₹800. Now the fair value of Investment is Rs 1200. At what value should it be recorded and how much gain will be credited to profit and loss account.

options.A: No change is required and it will continue at ₹800
options.B: Current investment will be recorded at ₹1000 and gain of ₹200 will be credited to profit and loss account.
options.C: Current investment will be recorded at ₹1200 and gain of ₹400 will be credited to profit and loss account.
options.D: Current investment will be recorded at ₹1200 but no gain will be credited to profit and loss account.

answer_html: Answer: (B) Current investment will be recorded at ₹1,000 and gain of ₹200 will be credited to profit and loss account — under AS 13, the investment was initially carried at the lower of cost (₹1,000) and fair value (₹800), i.e. ₹800. When fair value subsequently rises to ₹1,200, the carrying amount can be written back up, but only as far as the original cost (₹1,000) — never above it, even though the new fair value is higher. The write-back from ₹800 to ₹1,000 is a gain of ₹200 credited to profit and loss.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.6): Current investment written up only to original cost, never above cost, even if fair value later exceeds cost

case_facts_html:
A company engaged in refining, transportation, and marketing of petroleum products, during the financial year ended 31st March, 2025, acquired a controlling interest in another public sector undertaking from the Government of India at ₹1,551 per share. The book value and market value of the shares as of 18th February, 2025 were ₹192.58 and ₹876 per share, respectively. The company paid a strategic premium of ₹675 per share due to various tangible and intangible factors.

The company classified the acquired shares as long-term strategic investments and accounted for them at cost (₹1,551 per share); no provision for diminution in value was made. Schedule III requires the aggregate market value of quoted shares to be disclosed, and this has been reflected. On 28th March, 2025, the market price was ₹880 per share. By 18th July, the price had dropped to ₹300. Management believes the decline is not permanent, given strategic and synergy benefits expected, and hence no provision for diminution has been made.

Based on the information given above, answer Question Nos. 10–13.
question_html: Is the accounting treatment of recording the investment 'at cost' without providing for diminution correct as per AS 13?

options.A: Yes, as the investment is classified as long-term.
options.B: Yes, provided the decline in value is not other than temporary.
options.C: No, the market value must always be considered for long-term investments.
options.D: No, a provision for diminution must be made regardless of the cause of decline.

answer_html: Answer: (B) — AS 13 requires long-term investments to be carried at cost, with a provision only for a decline that is other than temporary; classification as long-term alone does not exempt an entity from testing for a permanent diminution.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.4): Long-term investments carried at cost, written down only for other-than-temporary decline

A company engaged in refining, transportation, and marketing of petroleum products, during the financial year ended 31st March, 2025, acquired a controlling interest in another public sector undertaking from the Government of India at ₹1,551 per share. Based on the information given above, answer Question Nos. 10–13.
question_html: How should the company assess whether the decline in market value is other than temporary?

options.A: Based solely on the market price on the balance sheet date.
options.B: Based on a comparison of the market price with the book value of the shares.
options.C: By considering all relevant factors, such as the financial health of the investee and expected benefits.

answer_html: Answer: (C) — AS 13 requires a holistic judgment considering all relevant factors (the investee's financial health, expected future benefits, reasons for the decline), not a mechanical single-date price comparison.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.4): Judgment-based assessment of other-than-temporary decline

question_html: If a provision for diminution in value is required, how should it be treated in the financial statements?

options.A: As a charge to the profit and loss account.
options.B: As deferred expenditure amortized over five years.
options.C: Directly adjusted against the investment account.
options.D: As a disclosure note without impacting the financial statements.

answer_html: Answer: (A) — a provision for other-than-temporary diminution is charged to the profit and loss account, per AS 13, not deferred or merely disclosed.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.4): Provision for diminution charged to profit and loss

Based on the information given above, answer Question Nos. 10–13.
question_html: Can the premium paid for strategic benefits be accounted for separately from the cost of investment?

options.A: Yes, it should be recorded as a separate intangible asset.
options.B: Yes, it can be disclosed as goodwill in the balance sheet.
options.C: No, it must be included in the cost of investment as per AS 13.
options.D: No, it must be expensed immediately in the profit and loss account.

answer_html: Answer: (C) — AS 13 requires the entire consideration paid, including any strategic premium, to be included in the cost of the investment; it cannot be split out as a separate intangible asset or goodwill.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.2): Cost of investment includes the entire acquisition consideration, including any strategic premium

case_facts_html:
Sun Limited has acquired 40% share in Moon Ltd. for ₹5,00,000 on 01.07.2024. Moon Ltd. is holding 40% stake in Star Limited. Sun Limited can exercise significant influence on Moon Limited. Moon Limited declared dividend of ₹80,000 for FY 2023-24 on 15.09.2024. For 2024-25, Moon Ltd. earned profit of ₹4,00,000 and declared dividend of ₹90,000 on 15.09.2025.

Answer the following questions based on the above.
question_html: What will be the carrying amount of investment in Separate Financial Statements of Sun Limited as on 31.03.2025?
answer_html: Answer: (A) ₹5,00,000 — in the investor's own separate (unconsolidated) financial statements, AS 13 requires investments in associates to be carried at cost, not equity-accounted; the equity method applies only in consolidated statements. Cost remains ₹5,00,000 unless a permanent diminution arises.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.4): Investments in associates carried at cost in separate financial statements, not equity-accounted

question_html: Pratham and Associates is a manufacturer of steel rods. It invests its profits by purchasing shares of listed companies in order to earn dividend income. It had purchased shares of Bharti Airtel Limited in FY 2018-19. However, it sold all the shares of Bharti Airtel Limited during the current year i.e. FY 2023-24. What amount would be disclosed in the profit and loss account for FY 2023-24?

options.A:
This transaction would not affect the profit and loss account since the primary business of
      the company is manufacturing, and not investment.
options.B: The carrying amount net of expenses would be disclosed in the profit and loss account.
options.C: The disposal proceeds net of expenses would be disclosed in the profit and loss account.
options.D:
The difference between the carrying amount and the disposal proceeds, net of expenses, would
      be disclosed in the profit and loss account.

answer_html: Answer: (D) — AS 13 requires the profit or loss on disposal of an investment to be recognised as the difference between the disposal proceeds and the carrying amount, net of expenses of disposal, in the profit and loss account. This applies regardless of whether investing is the entity's primary business — a manufacturing company that also holds investments is still subject to AS 13 for those investments.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.8): Disposal of investments - gain/loss is the difference between disposal proceeds and carrying amount, net of expenses

question_html: Suman Ltd. acquired 1000 shares of Sarika Ltd @ ₹150 each and paid brokerage @ 1%. In the same financial year, Sarika Ltd. issued bonus shares at one share for every four shares held by shareholders. Suman Ltd. sold 500 shares in the month of March in the same year and paid 1% brokerage, what will be the carrying value of investment in Sarika Ltd after sale of shares as per AS 13.
answer_html: Answer: (iii) ₹90,900 — cost of original acquisition including brokerage = 1,000 × ₹150 × 1.01 = ₹1,51,500. Bonus issue of 1 share per 4 held adds 250 shares at nil additional cost, so the holding becomes 1,250 shares at the same total cost of ₹1,51,500 (average cost per share = ₹1,51,500/1,250 = ₹121.20). AS 13 does not recognise a separate cost for bonus shares – the total cost is simply re-averaged over the enlarged holding. After selling 500 shares (brokerage on the sale affects the sale proceeds/profit figure, not the carrying cost of the remaining shares), the remaining 750 shares carry forward at average cost: 750 × ₹121.20 = ₹90,900.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.5): Bonus shares added at nil cost, re-averaging total cost over the enlarged holding, then valuing the remaining balance after a partial sale

case_facts_html:
Health India Limited (HIL), incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, is engaged in the production and distribution of medicines. It has manufacturing plants at Baddi (Himachal Pradesh) and Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh). It also imports medicines from Pharma Inc. New York (United States).

On 1st Jan 2024, HIL sold 2,00,000 strips of Medicine to Dee Limited for ₹50 Lakhs on 60 days of credit. Cost per strip of this medicine, was ₹20 (i.e. total cost ₹40 Lakhs, 2,00,000 strips @ ₹20). Dee Ltd. paid 20% of the amount due on 5th January, 2024. In March 2024, Dee Limited is having significant cash flow issues and is trying to raise funds through bank loan to run its operations. However, it is unable to do so and not able to release payment to HIL on due date. Subsequent to this, it has gone under liquidation on 15th March, 2024. At the time when medicine was sold by HIL to Dee Limited, there was no reason for HIL to believe that it will not be able to collect the sales proceeds from Dee Limited in future.

On 1st April, 2023 HIL has made an investment of ₹200 Lakhs in the equity shares of Rose Limited of which 50% is made in the long-term category i.e. long-term investment and rest as temporary investment i.e. current investment. The realisable value of all such investments on 31st March, 2024 becomes ₹50 Lakhs as Rose Limited lost a copyright. From the given market conditions, it is apparent that the reduction in the value of investment is not temporary in nature.

HIL imported medicine from Pharma Inc. for a sum of US $2,50,000 on 1st January, 2024. HIL released full payment on 17th April, 2024 to Medicine Ltd. The exchange rates are as follows: 1st April, 2023 ₹76 per $; 1st January, 2024 ₹81 per $; 31st March, 2024 ₹80 per $; 17th April, 2024 ₹79 per $.

HIL is working on a strategic plan to close the production unit of Bhopal due to change in technology. The board of directors approved the closure of Bhopal Plant on 1st March, 2024. The company did a formal announcement regarding closure to the affected parties on 10th March, 2024. The company entered into a binding-sale agreement on 21 April, 2024.

Reporting date of the company is 31st March, 2024. Based on the information given in the above Case Scenario, answer Question Nos. 6–9.
question_html: How will you recognize the reduction in the value of the investments in the financial statements for the year ended 31st March 2024 as per AS 13 (Revised)?

options.A: The reduction of ₹ 50 Lakhs in the carrying value of current investment will be charged to the profit and loss account. There will be no impact on the value of long-term investments.
options.B: The reduction of ₹ 75 Lakhs in the carrying value of current investment will be charged to the profit and loss account. There will be no impact on the value of long-term investments.
options.C: The reduction of ₹ 75 Lakhs in the carrying value of current investment will be charged to the profit and loss account. The reduction of ₹ 75 Lakhs in the carrying value of long-term investment will also be charged to the profit and loss account.
options.D: The reduction of ₹ 75 Lakhs in the carrying value of current investment will be charged to the profit and loss account. The reduction of ₹ 75 Lakhs in the carrying value of long-term investment will also be charged to capital reserve account.

answer_html: Answer: (C)
topic_text: AS 13 — Accounting for Investments (3.6): Carrying amount - current vs long-term investments, other than temporary decline

question_html: Pratham and Associates is a manufacturer of steel rods. It invests its profits by purchasing shares of listed companies in order to earn dividend income. It had purchased shares of Bharti Airtel Limited in FY 2020-21. However, it sold all the shares of Bharti Airtel Limited during the current year i.e. FY 2025-26. What amount would be disclosed in the profit and loss account for FY 2025-26?

options.A: This transaction would not affect the profit and loss account since the primary business of the company is manufacturing, and not investment.
options.B: The carrying amount net of expenses would be disclosed in the profit and loss account.
options.C: The disposal proceeds net of expenses would be disclosed in the profit and loss account.
options.D: The difference between the carrying amount and the disposal proceeds, net of expenses, would be disclosed in the profit and loss account.

answer_html: Answer: (D)
topic_text: AS 13 — Accounting for Investments (3.8): Disposal of investments - gain/loss recognised in P&L regardless of principal business

question_html: Cost of current investment acquired was ₹1,00,000 but the fair value was ₹80,000. The Investment was recorded at ₹80,000. Now the fair value of Investment is ₹1,20,000. At what value should it be recorded and how much gain will be credited to profit and loss account.

options.A: No change is required and it will continue at ₹80,000
options.B: Current investment will be recorded at ₹1,00,000 and gain of ₹20,000 will be credited to profit and loss account.
options.C: Current investment will be recorded at ₹1,20,000 and gain of ₹40,000 will be credited to profit and loss account.
options.D: Current investment will be recorded at ₹1,20,000 but no gain will be credited to profit and loss account.

answer_html: Answer: (B) Recorded at ₹1,00,000, gain of ₹20,000 credited to P&L — AS 13 carries current investments at the lower of cost and fair value; a rise in fair value above cost is never recognised (prudence), so the carrying amount can be written back up only as far as original cost (₹1,00,000), not to the full ₹1,20,000 fair value. The gain recognised (₹1,00,000 − ₹80,000 = ₹20,000) is simply the reversal of the earlier write-down, not an unrealised gain above cost.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.6): Current investment carrying value write-back capped at original cost, never above cost

question_html: Securities held as stock-in-trade held by an entity are:

options.C: May or may not be Investments

answer_html: Answer: (B) Not Investments — AS 13 defines Investments as assets held for earning income (dividends/interest/rentals), capital appreciation, or other benefits, not for trading. Securities held as stock-in-trade are held for sale in the ordinary course of business and fall under AS 2 (inventory), not AS 13.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.1-3.2): Securities held as stock-in-trade are excluded from the definition of Investments

case_facts_html:
Year 1

  • Mr. Lal purchased 1,000 equity shares of ₹100 each in a X Company @ ₹125 each from a stock broker who charged 2% brokerage. At the end of year 1 the market value of these shares is ₹1,50,000. He incurred 50 paise per ₹100 as cost of shares transfer stamps.
  • He also purchased gold for ₹5,00,000 for holding for long term perspective and by year end its value became ₹5,50,000.

Year 2

  • X Company issued bonus shares in the ratio of 1:1. At the end of year 2 market value of 2,000 shares of X Ltd. (including bonus shares) is still ₹1,50,000.
  • At the end of year 2, value of gold purchased is ₹6,50,000.
  • Mr. Lal sold the bonus shares for ₹110 per share during the year.

Answer the following questions on the basis of above information.
question_html: At the end of year 1, what will be the value of the investment in equity shares in the financial statements:
answer_html: Answer: (A) ₹1,28,125 — cost of investment = purchase price (1,000 × ₹125 = ₹1,25,000) + brokerage @2% (₹2,500) + share transfer stamp duty @0.5% of purchase price (₹625) = ₹1,28,125. Per AS 13, a long-term investment is carried at this cost even though the year-end market value (₹1,50,000) is higher — unrealised gains on long-term investments are never recognised.
topic_text: AS 13 — Accounting for Investments (3.5/3.6): Cost of investment includes incidental acquisition charges; long-term investments carried at cost

A pro-rata (cum-bonus) cost-averaging treatment of the 1:1 bonus issue — spreading the original ₹1,28,125 cost over the enlarged 2,000-share holding (₹64.0625/share) and removing the cost of the 1,000 bonus shares sold during the year — would instead value the remaining 1,000-share holding at ₹64,062.50, which is not among this sub-question's own printed options. The letter (A) is reproduced verbatim from the source answer key; see the extraction-note for the unresolved tension this created.
topic_text: AS 13 — Accounting for Investments (3.5/3.6): Carrying value of remaining holding after a bonus issue and part-disposal

question_html: At the end of year 2, what will be the value of the investment in Gold in the financial statements:
answer_html: Answer: (A) ₹5,00,000 — gold held for long-term investment purposes is a long-term investment under AS 13, carried at cost. Since its value has moved favourably (upward, not a decline), there is no basis to write it down, and AS 13 does not permit writing a long-term investment up to a higher market value either. It therefore remains at its original cost.

question_html: How much profit was earned on sale of bonus shares by Mr. Lal:
answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹45,937.50 — under the pro-rata (cum-bonus) cost-averaging treatment, the original cost of ₹1,28,125 is spread evenly over the enlarged 2,000-share holding once the 1:1 bonus is received, giving a cost of ₹64.0625 per share (i.e. half the original cost, ₹64,062.50, notionally attributable to the 1,000 bonus shares). Profit on sale of the 1,000 bonus shares @₹110 = sale proceeds ₹1,10,000 − apportioned cost ₹64,062.50 = ₹45,937.50.
topic_text: AS 13 — Accounting for Investments (3.5): Cost of a bonus issue apportioned pro-rata across the enlarged holding, not treated as nil

case_facts_html:
Health India Limited (HIL), incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, is engaged in the production and distribution of medicines. It has manufacturing plants at Baddi (Himachal Pradesh) and Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh). It also imports medicines from Pharma Inc. New York (United States).

On 1st Jan 2024, HIL sold 2,00,000 strips of Medicine to Dee Limited for ₹50 Lakhs on 60 days of credit. Cost per strip of this medicine, was ₹20. (i.e.) total cost ₹40 Lakhs (2,00,000 strips@₹20). Dee Ltd. paid 20% of the amount due on 5th January, 2024. In March 2024, Dee Limited is having significant cash flow issues and is trying to raise funds through bank loan to run its operations. However, it is unable to do so and not able to release payment to HIL on due date. Subsequent to this, it has gone under liquidation on 15th March, 2024. At the time when medicine was sold by HIL to Dee Limited, there was no reason for HIL to believe that it will not be able to collect the sales proceeds from Dee Limited in future.

On 1st April, 2023 HIL has made an investment of ₹200 Lakhs in the equity shares of Rose Limited of which 50% is made in the long-term category i.e. long-term investment and rest as temporary investment i.e. current investment. The realisable value of all such investments on 31st March, 2024 becomes ₹50 Lakhs as Rose Limited lost a copyright. From the given market conditions, it is apparent that the reduction in the value of investment is not temporary in nature.

HIL imported medicine from Pharma Inc. for a sum. of US $ 2,50,000 on 1st January, 2024. HIL released full payment on 17th April, 2024 to Medicine Ltd. The exchange rates are as follows:

Exchange rate per $
1st April, 2023₹76
1st January, 2024₹81
31st March, 2024₹80
17th April, 2024₹79

HIL is working on a strategic plan to close the production unit of Bhopal due to change in technology. The board of directors approved the closure of Bhopal Plan on 1st March, 2024. The company did a formal announcement regarding closure to the affected parties on 10th March, 2024. The company entered into a binding-sale agreement on 21 April, 2024.

Reporting date of the company is 31st March, 2024.

Based on the information given in the above Case Scenario, answer the following Question No. 6 to 9.
question_html: How will you recognize the reduction in the value of the investments in the financial statements for the year ended 31st March 2024 as per AS 13 (Revised)?

options.A: The reduction of ₹50 Lakhs in the carrying value of current investment will be charged to the profit and loss account. There will be no impact on the value of long-term investments.
options.B: The reduction of ₹75 Lakhs in the carrying value of current investment will be charged to the profit and loss account. There will be no impact on the value of long-term investments.
options.C: The reduction of ₹75 Lakhs in the carrying value of current investment will be charged to the profit and loss account. The reduction of ₹75 Lakhs in the carrying value of long-term investment will also be charged to the profit and loss account.
options.D: The reduction of ₹75 Lakhs in the carrying value of current investment will be charged to the profit and loss account. The reduction of ₹75 Lakhs in the carrying value of long-term investment will also be charged to capital reserve account.

answer_html: Answer: (C) Both the ₹75 lakh reduction in the current investment and the ₹75 lakh reduction in the long-term investment are charged to the Profit and Loss Account. The ₹200 lakh investment was split equally (₹100 lakhs current, ₹100 lakhs long-term); realisable value fell to ₹50 lakhs total, split proportionately ₹25 lakhs each, i.e. a ₹75 lakh fall on each half. Current investments are always carried at the lower of cost and fair value, so the ₹75 lakh fall goes to P&L. Because the fall in the long-term investment is explicitly stated to be "other than temporary" in nature, AS 13 requires that decline to also be charged to the Profit and Loss Account — a capital reserve credit/debit is not the mechanism AS 13 uses for investment write-downs.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.6): Current investments carried at lower of cost and fair value; an other-than-temporary decline in a long-term investment is also charged to the profit and loss account

case_facts_html:
Unicorn Limited manufactures building material. It took a loan of ₹60 Lakhs @10% p.a. on 1st August, 2025 to purchase raw material, and on the same day purchased 40,000 units of raw material @ ₹125 per unit (2 units of raw material per unit of finished goods). On 31st March, 2026: (i) 10,000 units of finished goods produced; (ii) NRV of finished goods ₹300/unit; (iii) Net replacement value of raw material ₹100/unit; (iv) Labour and variable overheads ₹10,00,000 for 10,000 units; (v) all finished goods produced remained in stock; (vi) no opening stock of raw material or finished goods.

Unicorn Limited used 15,000 units of raw material to construct an asset (Qualifying Asset). Labour and other overhead charges for construction ₹9,00,000. Paid ₹1,50,000 to install the asset at factory premises.

Unicorn Limited used the balance loan proceeds of ₹10,00,000 to invest in Equity shares of Royal Limited: 90,000 equity shares (Face value ₹10 each) for ₹10,00,000 on 25th March, 2026. Royal Limited declared and paid dividend @20% on 30th March 2026 for the year 2024-25.

A fraud of ₹2,80,000 done by the cashier of Unicorn Limited in January, 2026 was detected in April, 2026. The financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2026 were approved by the Board of Directors on 1st May, 2026.

Based on the information given in the above case scenario, answer Question Nos. 6–9.
question_html: What will be the carrying amount of investment as on 31st March, 2026 as per AS 13 and the treatment of dividend received from Royal Limited?

options.A: Carrying amount ₹7,20,000 and dividend deducted from the nominal value of investment.
options.B: Carrying amount ₹9,00,000 and dividend credited to Profit and Loss account.
options.C: Carrying amount ₹10,00,000 and dividend credited to Profit and Loss account.
options.D: Carrying amount ₹8,20,000 and dividend deducted from the cost of the investment.

answer_html: Answer: (D) — the dividend received relates to the pre-acquisition period (declared for FY 2024-25, on shares acquired 25th March, 2026), so it is treated as a recovery of cost, reducing the carrying amount rather than being credited to P&L.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.5): Pre-acquisition dividend treated as a recovery of cost, deducted from carrying cost

case_facts_html:
Mr. Vikram took a loan of ₹6,00,000 carrying interest @ 10% p.a. on 1st August, 2023 to purchase raw material. He purchased 4000 units of raw material @ ₹125 per unit. Replacement cost of raw material as on 31 March, 2024 is ₹100 per unit. Labour charges and variable overheads incurred are ₹1,00,000 to produce 1000 units of finished goods.

1000 units of Finished goods are produced with raw material (for every unit of finished goods produced, 2 units of raw material are required). Net realizable value of finished good is ₹300 per unit. All the finished goods produced are lying in stock as on 31 March, 2024.

There is no opening stock of raw material and finished goods.

Mr. Vikram used 1500 units of raw material to construct an Asset (Qualifying Asset). Labour and other overhead charges incurred on construction of asset are ₹90,000. Mr. Vikram also paid ₹15,000 to install the asset at Factory premises. Mr. Vikram used Balance of loan proceeds of ₹1,00,000 to invest in Equity Shares of P. Ltd. He purchased 9,000 Equity shares (Face Value ₹10 each) for ₹1,00,000 on 25th March, 2024.

The P. Ltd declared and paid dividend @ 20% on 30th March for the year 2023-24.

Based on the information given in above Case Scenario, answer the following Question No. 1-4:
question_html: What is the carrying amount of investment as on 31st March, 2024 as per AS 13 and suggest the treatment of dividend received from P. Ltd.?

options.A: Carrying amount of Investment as on 31st March, 2024 is ₹72,000 and the dividend is deducted from the nominal value of investment.
options.B: Carrying amount of Investment as on 31st March, 2024 is ₹90,000 and the dividend is credited to Profit & Loss A/c.
options.C: Carrying amount of Investment as on 31st March, 2024 is ₹1,00,000 and the dividend is credited to Profit & Loss A/c.
options.D: Carrying amount of Investment as on 31st March, 2024 is ₹82,000 and the dividend is deducted from the cost of investment.

answer_html: Answer: (D) ₹82,000, dividend deducted from cost — the 9,000 shares were purchased on 25th March 2024, only five days before the 30th March dividend declaration for the whole of FY 2023-24. Since the dividend substantially relates to a pre-acquisition period, AS 13 requires it to be treated as a recovery of the cost of investment, not as income. Dividend received = 20% × ₹10 face value × 9,000 shares = ₹18,000. Carrying amount = ₹1,00,000 − ₹18,000 = ₹82,000.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.5): Pre-acquisition dividend received treated as a recovery of the cost of investment, not credited to Profit and Loss

question_html: Cost of a current investment acquired was ₹1000 but fair value was ₹800; recorded at ₹800. Now fair value of the investment is ₹1200. At what value should it be recorded, and how much gain credited to profit and loss?

options.B: Recorded at ₹1000 and gain of ₹200 credited to P&L.
options.C: Recorded at ₹1200 and gain of ₹400 credited to P&L.
options.D: Recorded at ₹1200 but no gain credited to P&L.

answer_html: Answer: (ii) — current investments are carried at the lower of cost and fair value; even though fair value has now risen to ₹1,200 (above cost), the investment cannot be marked up beyond its original cost of ₹1,000. The carrying value is restored from ₹800 to ₹1,000 (the ceiling), recognising a gain of ₹200 (1,000−800) — the further rise from 1,000 to 1,200 is unrealised and not recognised.
topic_text: AS 13 (3.3): Current investments carried at the lower of cost and fair value - never marked up beyond original cost
